title: Let's encrypt TLS Challenge failing when behind a traefik TCP Router
body:
### Welcome!

- [X] Yes, I've searched similar issues on [GitHub](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues) and didn't find any.
- [X] Yes, I've searched similar issues on the [Traefik community forum](https://<redacted-host>) and didn't find any.

### What did you do?

I have multiple servers in my Network and one public static IP. The firewall is forwarding all traffic to `Server 1` on ports 80 and 443. `Server 1` has multiple TCP Router in place to send the traffic to `Server 2` and `Server 3` which look live this:

```
tcp:
    routers:
        server_2:
            entrypoints:
                - websecure
            rule: HostSNIRegexp(`^.+\.server2\.subdomain\.example\.com$`)
            tls:
                passthrough: true
            service: server_2
    services:
        server_2:
            loadBalancer:
                proxyProtocol:
                    version: 2
                servers:
                    - address: 172.16.10.12:443
```

and

```
tcp:
    routers:
        server_3:
            entrypoints:
                - websecure
            rule: HostSNIRegexp(`^.+\.server3\.subdomain\.example\.com$`)
            tls:
                passthrough: true
            service: server_3
    services:
        server_3:
            loadBalancer:
                proxyProtocol:
                    version: 2
                servers:
                    - address: 172.16.10.13:443
```

On `Server 2` and` Server 3` lets's encrypt is configures like this:

```
certificatesResolvers:
    letsencrypt-tls:
        acme:
            email: <email-scrubbed>
            storage: /letsencrypt/acme.json
            tlsChallenge: true 
```

If try to create a Certificate on `Server 2` or `Server 3` for example `www.app.server2.subdomain.example.com` and `app.server2.subdomain.example.com` it always fails for the domain with the `www` prefix. With a `error 400` code.

**Edit**
it looks like all certification request are failing not only the one with the `www` prefix, which was reported because it was the first to process.

On `Server 1` which is facing directly to the internet the problem is not present.

### What did you see instead?

comments.author: rtribotte
comments.body:
Hello @reporter @CybotTM @participant3 @participant2,

As @participant2 mentioned, this behavior is due to changes in https://github.com/traefik/traefik/pull/10536.
This is an intended behavior and was introduced to make Traefik more secure in some context (multi-tenancy).

However, we think we could introduce an option to allow the "insecure" mode.
We are also considering enforcing this only when Traefik is configured to handle ACME TLS challenges.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
> @participant3 Thanks for your feedback. Are you using a TLS resolver with Traefik? We are wondering if simply allowing the TLS challenge passthrough when no TLS resolver is configured is enough in your situation.

Not really, since my configuration is shared between pretty much all my traefik instances.
The insecure flag for passthing through tls challenges as well would actually better suite my needs.

I'm using traefik both as a reverse proxy for my docker application as well as a network wide reverse proxy to allow things like a NAS to obtain a Let's encrypt Certificate.

To me the TLS-Passthrough is one of traefiks killer-features. It's just so convinient to share Port 443 without much reconfiguration needed on third party vm images. Some applications just assume they will handle TLS themselves and I actually like having those connections encrypted, even if it is inside my "secure" local network.

Here's a little diagram about how I use traefik:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    
internet[Internet]
network-traefik[Network Traefik]
internet -->|Port 443 / 80| network-traefik
network-traefik -->|Port 443\nTLS-Passthrough| docker-traefik1[Docker Traefik 1]
network-traefik -->|Port 443\nTLS-Passthrough| docker-traefik2[Docker Traefik 2]
network-traefik -->|Port 443\nTLS-Passthrough| docker-traefik3[Docker Traefik 3]

network-traefik -->|Port 80\nPathprefix: /.well-known/acme-challenge| nas[NAS]
network-traefik -->|Port 80 / 443\nTLS-Passthrough\nPathprefix: /.well-known/acme-challenge| non-docker-host[Non Docker Host]
```

To make this easier I actually built myself a very basic Web-UI to configure routes so I don't have to use nano in the command line.

https://github.com/Rahn-IT/traefik-gui (Warning: very janky)

I really love traefik because it automagically handles my docker routing with just a few labels and I can easily share my external Port 443 **without breaking the TLS encryption inside my local network** - I mean how cool is that? No other reverse proxy combines this feature set with such elegance as traefik.

comments.author: rtribotte
comments.body:
Hello @participant3 @reporter @CybotTM @participant5,

Thanks for all the feedback!

We're not against introducing an option, but first we want to make sure that the solution from #10981 doesn't fit your use cases.

@CybotTM We introduced this breaking change as a fix because of security concerns we had regarding potential hijacking of certificate negotiation in a multi-tenant environment.
I have to admit that we probably moved too fast on this issue, because in the end we came to the conclusion that Traefik should not be considered secure "out of the box" when used to expose routes of multiple clients in a multi-tenant environment, simply because Traefik does not provide/enforce client isolation.

Now that we have introduced this behavior, we are reluctant to undo it and prefer to mitigate the use case exposed in this issue, if possible, without introducing yet another option.

As of today, regarding the ACME HTTP challenge, as long as no HTTP challenge resolver is configured, it is possible for a user to handle the challenge with a custom HTTP router.
Once an HTTP challenge resolver is configured, the HTTP challenge resolver handler would preempt any request on the `/.well-known/` path.

With #10981, we wanted to introduce the same tweak, so that as long as no TLS challenge resolver (and only this one) is configured, using custom TLS pass-through router would be possible without any additional configuration.

@participant3 In the setup you shared, it seems doable not to declare the TLS challenge resolver on the "gateway" `Network Traefik` instance, WDYT?

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
> @CybotTM We introduced this breaking change as a fix because of security concerns we had regarding potential hijacking of certificate negotiation in a multi-tenant environment.
I have to admit that we probably moved too fast on this issue, because in the end we came to the conclusion that Traefik should not be considered secure "out of the box" when used to expose routes of multiple clients in a multi-tenant environment, simply because Traefik does not provide/enforce client isolation.

So you're blocking this because in theory a compromised downstream application that is not supposed to have access to TLS certificates should not be able to generate a valid certificate that could then be used for additional attacks?

If I got this wrong, I'd be interested to hear more about your concerns. As far as I understand, the TLS challenge is already only handed through to the routers which actually match the SNI. Which means I can only try to obtain certificates for my own domain, just like the HTTP challenge. And that also only works then TLS passthrough is on. When it's off the TLS tunnel is terminated before reaching the target, thus blocking of the alpn request, right?

> @participant3 In the setup you shared, it seems doable not to declare the TLS challenge resolver on the "gateway" Network Traefik instance, WDYT?

In theory yes, but as I've said: my traefik configurations share their configuration and this would make matters more complicated than they already are. This also breaks apart if I had 3 traefik instances in a row.

I think the best option would still be the `insecure` option. Although I'd name it more explicitly. Maybe `allow_acme_challenge` or `passthrough_acme_challenge`?

In a full example this could look like this:

```yaml
tcp:
    routers:
        server_3:
            entrypoints:
                - websecure
            rule: HostSNIRegexp(`^.+\.server3\.example\.com$`)
            tls:
                passthrough:
                    allow_acme_challenge: true
            service: server_3
```

If passthrough is set to `true` you just fall back to your default options setting `allow_acme_challenge` to `false`.

---

If that is to much work, how about adding a static option or environment variable to bypass the check from #10536 for all routers?

Maybe something like `tls_passthrough_allow_acme_challenge` ?

People like me could just enable this option to get the old behaviour back - since I'm not in a multi-tentant environment I won't have any problems.

Edit: The HTTP Option also doesn't work when only passing through Port 443 from the internet, which I personally like to do if I can - less attack surface is always a win.

comments.author: rtribotte
comments.body:
@participant3 Thanks a lot for the thorough feedback!

> If I got this wrong, I'd be interested to hear more about your concerns. As far as I understand, the TLS challenge is already only handed through to the routers which actually match the SNI. Which means I can only try to obtain certificates for my own domain, just like the HTTP challenge. And that also only works then TLS passthrough is on. When it's off the TLS tunnel is terminated before reaching the target, thus blocking of the alpn request, right?

The attack would essentially be that on a Traefik instance serving multiple domains for multiple clients, a client could initiate and preempt a challenge for a domain that he is not the owner, but belongs to another client. This would take advantage of the DNS configuration targeting the Traefik instance to obtain a certificate for a domain it doesn't own, and probably try to use it to serve some malicious services.

If the main reason for introducing this option is not to have to differentiate static configurations between Traefik instances, we have to say that we are not yet convinced. And using the same static configuration for all Traefik instances (which have different responsibilities) is certainly not something we would recommend.
We remain open to introducing an option and would like your feedback on this, but it would most likely be a static option and not a per router configuration.

comments.author: participant8
comments.body:
The documentation for this new behaviour switch could do with being clearer.

As background, in my case I am trying to configure Traefik with *some* routers doing a full pass-through including ACME pass-through (some to further Traefik instances, some to other services that manage their own ACME). This was working in a previous Traefik version, I'm just trying to restore the previous behaviour. I've read the issue, describing why and when the behaviour was changed. What I'm missing is a precise description. I don't ask here just to get a one-off answer for my particular case today, I want to ask that the docs be clarified so it's clear for everyone every time.

So far it seems there is just [this documentation of `AllowACMEByPass`](https://<redacted-host>/traefik/routing/entrypoints/#allowacmebypass) entrypoint option, and some abbreviations of that in a couple of other places.

1. It says it determines if "a [...] router can handle"... but it is an entrypoint option so it applies to many routers. It needs to state the rule that determines what kind of handling applies to *each specific* router. In other words, I don't just want to know how to configure Traefik such that "a (unspecified) router can handle" but I want to decide which particular routers will pass through ACME and which will handle it for me. (I gather from previous reading around, that the decision is also related to whether a certificate resolver is configured at all (globally) and/or on the router specifically; but it needs to be stated as a precise rule.)

2. Clarify which *types of routers* this affects. (I happen to know it's particularly useful for TLS pass-through routers, as that's my use case. It ought to make clear whether it also affects non-TLS and/or non-passthrough routers.)

3. There are now two kinds of *TLS pass-through*: where ACME is handled by (this instance of) Traefik, and where ACME is passed through along with the rest of the traffic. The [documentation of router option `passthrough`](https://<redacted-host>/traefik/routing/routers/#passthrough) should now state that there are these two kinds, and should say (or point to documentation on) how to select the desired kind.

For the record, this is what the documentation said at the time when I posted this message:

> ## AllowACMEByPass[¶](https://<redacted-host>/traefik/routing/entrypoints/#allowacmebypass)
> 
> *Optional, Default=false*
> 
> `allowACMEByPass` determines whether a user defined router can handle ACME TLS or HTTP challenges instead of the Traefik dedicated one. This option can be used when a Traefik instance has one or more certificate resolvers configured, but is also used to route challenges connections/requests to services that could also initiate their own ACME challenges.
No Certificate Resolvers configured
> 
> It is not necessary to use the `allowACMEByPass' option certificate option if no certificate resolver is defined. In fact, Traefik will automatically allow ACME TLS or HTTP requests to be handled by custom routers in this case, since there can be no concurrency with its own challenge handlers.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
@participant8 Some of what you describe was talked about here, but was ultimately not implemented as it was deemed to complicated.

> in my case I am trying to configure Traefik with some routers doing a full pass-through including ACME
As you can see in the documentation this is a per entry point option.
If you want traefik to behave as before you can just enable this option for all endpoints.

If this option is not enabled, traefik will check if something is an ACME challenge ans basically skip the default routing step and pass it straight to the ACME logic.

This does not really impact the behaviour of the routers, rather the default option bypasses normal routing. This switch instead forces the ACME challenge to pass **through** the routers.

This is how I understand it:
```mermaid
flowchart LR

Request --> acme{Is ACME challenge?}
acme -->|No| routing{Request matches Router?}
acme -->|Yes| allowbypass{Is Bypassing allowed?}
allowbypass -->|Yes|routing
routing -->|Yes| forward[Forward to service]
routing -->|No| acme2{Is ACME challenge?}
acme2 --> |No| 404[Error 404]
acme2 -->|Yes| acmeh
allowbypass -->|No| acmeh[Internal ACME Handler]
```

Feel free to correct me if this is found to be wrong.
